about.intro: cs-ui is open source: MIT licensed, code on GitHub, issues and changes in the open.
about.links.title: Links
about.principle1: Defaults first: a component with no arguments should already look right.
about.principle2: Tokens, not constants: color, spacing and radius come from one place.
about.principle3: Subscriptions, not broadcasts: only components that read state re-render.
about.principle4: Compose, don't configure: new looks come from composition, not a tenth boolean.
about.principles.desc: These rules decide what cs-ui looks like — and what it refuses to do.

about.runtime.title: Runtime
arch.intro: cs-ui doesn't replace Flet — it adds a layer on top: sharper defaults, subscribable theme and language, and a composable UI vocabulary.
arch.kinds.desc: Static ones subclass a control; stateful ones pair a data object with ui().
arch.kinds.note: Build stateful components inside @ft.component and pin them with use_ref. Otherwise a parent re-render recreates the object and the user's input is gone.
arch.kinds.title: Two kinds of components
arch.layers.point1: Controls — subclass Flet controls, change defaults only.
arch.layers.point2: State — use_state / use_ref / use_memo plus observable objects.
arch.layers.point3: Infrastructure — theme, i18n, routing, formatting, tokens.
arch.layers.point4: Application — pages only compose; they never touch the plumbing.
arch.layers.title: Layers
arch.perf.desc: Re-renders follow subscriptions; switching theme or language never rebuilds the tree.
arch.perf.point1: Only components that read use_t() / use_theme() re-render.
arch.perf.point2: Route changes keep the shell: top bar and sidebar stay mounted.
arch.perf.point3: Form instances are reused, so typing never recreates objects.
arch.perf.title: Performance
arch.providers.desc: Language outermost, theme next, router innermost — order decides the first frame.
arch.providers.tip: Providers memoize build(): switching language re-renders only components that called use_t(), so the tree — and your form state — survives.
arch.providers.title: Provider order
arch.routing.danger: render_views builds a view stack over page.overlay: MultiSelect flyouts and DateInput calendars silently stop working.
arch.routing.desc: Root-view rendering plus manage_views=False keeps overlays and flyouts alive.

arch.state.desc: Local state via hooks; cross-page state via a module-level observable singleton.
arch.state.point1: use_state — component-local state; change it and the component re-renders.
arch.state.point2: use_ref — pin an instance across renders; form controls live here.
arch.state.point3: use_memo — cache expensive work against dependencies.

resp.boot.desc: A window's startup size does not fire on_resize, and page.width in main() still holds the previous size. apply_responsive re-reads it a few times after the first frame, so once it has been called the class is right from then on; without it, use_responsive() stays at expanded — permanent sidebar, no wrapped header.
resp.boot.title: Booted narrow
resp.grid.desc: ResponsiveRow asks every child to carry its own breakpoint dictionary; Grid asks for one minimum cell width. “How narrow may a cell get” is a design fact; “how many columns per breakpoint” is the computed consequence and should not be retyped by hand.
resp.grid.tip: Column counts are sent as “virtual columns = cells per row” with each child spanning one, so equal widths come from structure rather than from 12 being divisible by 3. Five cells in a 12-column grid leave two columns that cannot be split.
resp.grid.title: Grid: name a minimum, not a count
resp.hook.desc: Reach for the hook only when the difference is structural (sidebar or not, table or cards). It repaints the component when the class changes, so do not do pixel math inside it — that belongs to the renderer.
resp.hook.title: When you need the class
resp.hook.warn: use_responsive() reflects the window width. A component may occupy only part of it (sidebar, split pane, dialog) — there it should measure itself. PageLayout and Descriptions use on_size_change and ignore the window.
resp.intro: Responsive design is not “add a narrow variant to every component” — it starts with one rule: who is allowed to judge width. Here the rule is structural changes in Python, continuous changes in the renderer. Reflowing a grid and stretching an element happen every frame — that is Flutter's job. “Should the sidebar collapse?” changes at most once a second — that is Python's job. Mixing them fails both ways: recomputing every frame stutters, and Flutter cannot see your business structure.
resp.live.desc: When the grid below reflows, Python does not run at all — the column count for every breakpoint was written in at build time, and reflow happens entirely in the renderer. That is what “leave continuous changes to Flutter” means.
resp.live.title: Drag it
resp.own.desc: The other half of responsive design is usually forgotten: narrow screens must fit, and wide screens must not stretch. Past roughly 75 characters per line the eye has to travel further and reading slows down; a form stretched to 2000px looks like a label on the far left and its input on the far right with a desert in between. Centre it and cap it.
resp.own.note: PageLayout's max_content_width switches itself off on narrow containers — capping width there would squeeze the content away. One piece of code: centred when wide, full-bleed when narrow, no second variant.
resp.own.title: Cap the width on wide screens
resp.rules.desc: Breakpoints, window classes, notification timing and what you may touch — once these four are fixed, components behave consistently:
resp.rules.point1: Breakpoints are identical to flet's ResponsiveRow (0 / 576 / 768 / 992 / 1200 / 1400). A second set of boundaries produces the classic mismatch: the grid already reflowed, the page still thinks it is narrow.
resp.rules.point2: Six breakpoints collapse into three window classes: compact (< 768), medium (768–1199), expanded (≥ 1200). Layout strategy needs exactly these three — finer splits chop one decision into fragments.
resp.rules.point3: Only the window class triggers a repaint, and only when it actually changes. Width changes on every pixel while dragging; notifying each time turns the UI into a slideshow.
resp.rules.point4: At runtime, change properties only — never the tree. flet 1.1.2 does not guarantee that structural patches to an already-mounted tree reach the screen: replacing content, swapping a whole list, even toggling visible can leave Python correct and the screen unchanged — and the tree a component renders is frozen, so not even a child's properties can be touched. Decide structure at build time; to follow the window class, let an observable re-render the page (a component).
resp.rules.title: Four rules

theme.intro: A theme isn't a pile of color constants — it's subscribable state. Change the seed or the mode and the UI follows.
theme.live.desc: This panel uses the same tokens — it recolors the moment you switch.
theme.live.point2: Seed: one brand color becomes the whole M3 palette (46 roles).
theme.live.title: Live theme
theme.modes.desc: ThemeProvider writes both themes (page.theme and page.dark_theme) — switching mode swaps a ready-made tree instead of recomputing colors at runtime.
theme.modes.title: Light and dark
theme.palette.desc: Hand the seed to color_scheme_seed and Flutter derives the palette with tonalSpot — which turns #1F6FEB into #465D91, stripping half the brand chroma. So palette computes all 46 roles up front, one set per mode.
theme.palette.desc2: Any seed yields an isomorphic scheme: the eleven tone steps keep a constant ~0.075 lightness interval, hue drifts less than 4°, and the container ladder mirrors itself between modes.
theme.palette.point1: Hue never moves, only lightness: a brand color may be darkened to carry white text, but its hue must not change.
theme.palette.point2: Lightness is solved for contrast: 5:1 for accents on the surface, 7:1 for solid fills in dark mode — at equal tone, yellow and blue differ threefold in contrast.
theme.palette.point3: Neutrals carry a trace of the brand hue (chroma 0.006): Slate looks premium precisely because it is not a dead grey.
theme.palette.title: One seed → a whole scheme
theme.semantic.desc: success / warning / danger / info / neutral are decoupled from the theme:
theme.semantic.desc2: They keep ≥4.5:1 contrast in both modes, so status is always readable.
theme.semantic.title: Semantic colors
theme.surfaces.desc: Surfaces are a designed neutral ramp: near-white in light mode, deep slate in dark, with a trace of the brand hue in the grey (never a dead neutral). Cards are separated by 1px outlines and translucent overlays rather than by brute-forcing container tones.
theme.surfaces.title: Surfaces
theme.surfaces.tonal: Want visibly tinted surfaces? Set surfaces to tonal: the same ramp takes on more of the brand hue and no component changes.
theme.tokens.desc: Spacing, radius, type scale and elevation come from ui — no magic numbers in pages.
theme.tokens.scale_desc: The scales are finite: pick the nearest step instead of inventing numbers.
theme.tokens.title: Design tokens
theme.trap: Page components run a frame late, so a direct write flashes the old palette. Go through ThemeProvider and use_theme().
theme.trap_title: Never set page.theme in a page
